event_overview.title: About Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.subject: Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.summary: The Russia-Ukraine War is an ongoing interstate armed conflict that expanded into a full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, following fighting in eastern Ukraine that had persisted since 2014. It has involved ground combat, missile and air attacks, maritime operations, and long-range drone strikes affecting both Ukrainian territory and locations inside Russia. International institutions have documented extensive civilian harm and continued legal and diplomatic disputes arising from the conflict.

facts.label: Full-scale phase
facts.value: Russian armed forces launched a full-scale armed attack on Ukraine on February 24, 2022; the conflict followed an earlier phase of armed conflict in eastern Ukraine beginning in 2014.

facts.label: Parties and geography
facts.value: The principal belligerents are the Russian Federation and Ukraine. The war has affected Ukraine nationwide and has also included attacks and other military incidents beyond the front lines, including across the Russia-Ukraine border.

facts.label: International legal context
facts.value: The International Court of Justice ordered provisional measures on March 16, 2022, including that Russia immediately suspend the military operations it commenced in Ukraine on February 24, 2022; the order did not decide the merits of the underlying case.

facts.label: Civilian impact monitoring
facts.value: The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine documents conflict-related civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure, while cautioning that verified figures are incomplete and actual totals are likely higher.

story_report.summary: Elon Musk confirmed that he was behind speed restrictions on Starlink service in Ukraine, after normal speeds were restored. The restrictions had disrupted military operations, while Ukrainian officials said restored connectivity was important for frontline logistics and defense. The episode has also produced competing accounts of why services were limited and who authorized related Starshield measures, as Kyiv continues diplomatic efforts and seeks to open humanitarian access to Russian-occupied Oleshky.

sections.heading: Restrictions Disrupted Frontline Military Operations
sections.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine had tested both services and that restored speeds were important for logistics at the front and for defense against jet-powered Shahed drones. Reuters reported that the cap cut off Starshield receivers mounted on objects moving faster than 160 km/h, putting some drone-combat and air-defense missions at risk. AP also reported that Ukrainian commanders described lost drones and disrupted missions during the restrictions.

sections.heading: Accounts Differ Over Restriction Authority
sections.body: Musk said SpaceX throttled civilian Starlink because Ukraine had used it for offensive drone strikes in violation of its terms, while saying changes to Starshield were controlled by the U.S. government. Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense-technology adviser to Zelenskyy, disputed that explanation, saying existing civilian-Starlink limits had already made offensive use impossible. Reuters reported conflicting accounts of the order’s origin, including claims of White House involvement and a report that Musk personally directed it; Donald Trump denied involvement and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said access decisions rested with SpaceX and Musk.

sections.heading: Ukraine Pursues Diplomacy and Oleshky Access
sections.body: Zelenskyy said Ukraine was preparing meetings in Europe with U.S. presidential envoys and European partners, with further diplomatic work expected the following week. AP reported that Russia had agreed to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv the following month. Zelenskyy also said an arrangement concerning Russian-occupied Oleshky was expected to be implemented soon, allowing food and medicine access and civilian departures, with Ukraine relying on U.S. mediation.

event_overview.title: About Protests in France
event_overview.subject: Protests in France
event_overview.summary: The event is a wave of nationwide demonstrations in France that grew from a student-led movement over conditions in secondary schools into broader protests over living costs, inflation and public services. Large peaceful marches on October 17, 2026 were accompanied in some locations by clashes, vandalism and looting, prompting local security measures and a national political response.

facts.label: Origins and stated grievances
facts.value: Reporting describes the movement as beginning with high-school student protests in late September 2026 over lycée conditions, then expanding to include concerns about the cost of living, inflation and public services.

facts.label: Major nationwide mobilization
facts.value: The principal nationwide demonstrations took place on Saturday, October 17, 2026; reporting distinguished the large peaceful marches from violent incidents that occurred on their margins in several cities.

facts.label: Participants and organization
facts.value: This is a decentralized social protest movement rather than a single event run by one organizer: participants reported across coverage include students, trade unions, Yellow Vest supporters, workers in several sectors and political activists.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Demonstrations and subsequent disorder were reported across France, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux; the event therefore involves both national political issues and locally imposed public-order measures.

facts.label: Legal framework for public demonstration
facts.value: French law requires prior declaration for processions, parades and other demonstrations on public roads. In general, organizers file between three and 15 clear days in advance with the relevant mayor or prefecture; authorities may prohibit a planned demonstration when they judge it likely to disturb public order.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate aftermath and official responses on October 18-19, 2026, including disruption in Paris and Marseille; it does not attempt to catalogue every protest, participant group, injury, arrest, damage claim or later legal proceeding.

story_report.summary: More than 400,000 people protested across France, with demonstrations centered on rising living costs and calls for greater school funding. The mobilization began around school staffing concerns before broadening, and was largely peaceful, though clashes erupted in Paris as the marches concluded. The government reported nearly 1,000 arrests, shifting the immediate aftermath toward investigations and legal processing while officials advanced education-related responses.

sections.heading: Education Demands and Government Response
sections.body: The movement began with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris, then expanded into demands for more education funding and assistance with fuel and other living costs. The Education Ministry said it had deployed more than 3,000 substitute teachers to high schools with the greatest need, authorized further hiring and allocated additional short-term replacement hours. The prime minister also assigned five workstreams on teacher absences, facilities, schedules, guidance and student participation, with initial decisions due by the end of October 2026. Student representatives said Macron had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue pending concrete measures.

sections.heading: Police Response and Further Protest Calls
sections.body: Before the October 24 mobilization, the Interior Ministry instructed prefects to assess organizers and proposed routes, and said demonstrations could be barred from areas at risk of renewed looting or destruction or redirected when discussions failed. The ministry said prosecutors and police would document alleged offenses, preserve evidence and quickly process arrested people for possible referral to justice; it later reported that several investigations had opened. At the Paris march, protesters called for an “Act III” demonstration on October 31, but this was a participant appeal rather than an official announcement or confirmed national plan.

event_overview.title: About Protests in France
event_overview.subject: Protests in France
event_overview.summary: The event is a wave of nationwide demonstrations in France that grew from a student-led movement over conditions in secondary schools into broader protests over living costs, inflation and public services. Large peaceful marches on October 17, 2026 were accompanied in some locations by clashes, vandalism and looting, prompting local security measures and a national political response.

facts.label: Origins and stated grievances
facts.value: Reporting describes the movement as beginning with high-school student protests in late September 2026 over lycée conditions, then expanding to include concerns about the cost of living, inflation and public services.

facts.label: Major nationwide mobilization
facts.value: The principal nationwide demonstrations took place on Saturday, October 17, 2026; reporting distinguished the large peaceful marches from violent incidents that occurred on their margins in several cities.

facts.label: Participants and organization
facts.value: This is a decentralized social protest movement rather than a single event run by one organizer: participants reported across coverage include students, trade unions, Yellow Vest supporters, workers in several sectors and political activists.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Demonstrations and subsequent disorder were reported across France, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux; the event therefore involves both national political issues and locally imposed public-order measures.

facts.label: Legal framework for public demonstration
facts.value: French law requires prior declaration for processions, parades and other demonstrations on public roads. In general, organizers file between three and 15 clear days in advance with the relevant mayor or prefecture; authorities may prohibit a planned demonstration when they judge it likely to disturb public order.

event_overview.title: About Yemen Conflict
event_overview.subject: Yemen Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Yemen conflict is a protracted political and armed struggle centered on the Houthi movement (Ansar Allah), Yemen’s internationally recognized government and other Yemeni armed and political actors. It intensified after the Houthis seized Sana’a in 2014 and became regionalized when a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015; United Nations-led efforts have sought a negotiated, Yemeni-led settlement.

facts.label: Origins and escalation
facts.value: The present phase escalated in mid-2014, when conflict between government forces, the Houthis and other armed groups intensified; Houthi forces and allied military units took Sana’a in September 2014.

facts.label: Regional intervention
facts.value: A coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened militarily on 26 March 2015 at the request of then-President Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi, transforming the conflict into a regionalized war.

facts.label: Main conflict setting
facts.value: The conflict is principally within Yemen, but it has also involved cross-border hostilities and regional actors; the UN describes it as involving the Houthis, government forces and other armed groups, with consequences for the wider region.

facts.label: UN peace process
facts.value: The Office of the UN Special Envoy for Yemen was established in 2012 to support a Yemeni political transition and has continued to mediate toward a nationwide ceasefire and inclusive political process. A UN-brokered truce began on 2 April 2022, was extended twice, and expired on 2 October 2022.

facts.label: International legal and monitoring frame
facts.value: UN Security Council resolution 2452, adopted on 16 January 2019, established the UN Mission to Support the Hudaydah Agreement (UNMHA) to help implement the Stockholm Agreement’s arrangements for Hudaydah, Salif and Ras Issa ports, including ceasefire monitoring, redeployments and mine action.

event_overview.title: About Protests in France
event_overview.subject: Protests in France
event_overview.summary: The event is a wave of nationwide demonstrations in France that grew from a student-led movement over conditions in secondary schools into broader protests over living costs, inflation and public services. Large peaceful marches on October 17, 2026 were accompanied in some locations by clashes, vandalism and looting, prompting local security measures and a national political response.

facts.label: Origins and stated grievances
facts.value: Reporting describes the movement as beginning with high-school student protests in late September 2026 over lycée conditions, then expanding to include concerns about the cost of living, inflation and public services.

facts.label: Major nationwide mobilization
facts.value: The principal nationwide demonstrations took place on Saturday, October 17, 2026; reporting distinguished the large peaceful marches from violent incidents that occurred on their margins in several cities.

facts.label: Participants and organization
facts.value: This is a decentralized social protest movement rather than a single event run by one organizer: participants reported across coverage include students, trade unions, Yellow Vest supporters, workers in several sectors and political activists.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Demonstrations and subsequent disorder were reported across France, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux; the event therefore involves both national political issues and locally imposed public-order measures.

facts.label: Legal framework for public demonstration
facts.value: French law requires prior declaration for processions, parades and other demonstrations on public roads. In general, organizers file between three and 15 clear days in advance with the relevant mayor or prefecture; authorities may prohibit a planned demonstration when they judge it likely to disturb public order.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate aftermath and official responses on October 18-19, 2026, including disruption in Paris and Marseille; it does not attempt to catalogue every protest, participant group, injury, arrest, damage claim or later legal proceeding.
